title: Psychology Foundations
description: Twenty-unit professional-style psychology foundation covering scientific method, brain and behaviour, consciousness, learning, memory, emotion, development, social and cultural psychology, mental-health literacy, sensation and perception, motivation, cognition, attachment, trauma, psychopathology, assessment, psychotherapy, health psychology and ethics.
creditNote: 20 internal Save One Soul formation credits. Professional-style breadth and study method; non-accredited and not a qualification, licence or evidence of competence to practise psychology, counselling or psychotherapy.

units.title: Psychology as a science
units.label: Educational study
objectives: Distinguish evidence, interpretation and personal opinion.
Apply the lesson to the case study and explain the limits of your conclusion.
paragraphs: Psychology studies behaviour and mental processes using systematic methods. A useful question must be clear enough to investigate: “Does practising recall improve next-week test performance?” is more testable than “What unlocks the whole mind?” Define what you mean by practice and performance before comparing results.

A correlation describes an association; it does not by itself establish that one thing caused another. Sleep, workload and health could affect both study habits and marks. Controlled studies can address some alternatives, while interviews and observation answer different questions. Sample size, representativeness, measurement and replication matter. Be cautious with a dramatic claim based on one small study or a testimonial. This course introduces ways to think critically; it does not prepare you to diagnose people or conduct unsupervised experiments on vulnerable participants.
units.assignment: A post claims that people who pray daily always have better memory. Identify two alternative explanations and describe an ethical way to study the association.

quiz.question: A correlation between sleep and grades proves what?
options: Sleep is the only cause of grades.
Every student needs identical sleep.
An association, without establishing causation by itself.
quiz.explanation: Other variables and study design affect causal conclusions.

quiz.question: Which question is most testable?
options: What single habit cures every problem?
Does a defined recall exercise change scores after one week?
Which method unlocks all human potential?
quiz.explanation: A testable question specifies observable variables.

units.title: Brain, body and behaviour
units.label: Educational study
objectives: Name major brain systems involved in planning, memory, emotion, reward, bodily drives and habit learning.
Explain why complex experiences such as fear, anger, lust, pride or addiction cannot be assigned to one brain region.
Apply the lesson to the case study and explain the limits of your conclusion.
paragraphs: The brain works through interacting networks rather than isolated moral modules. The prefrontal cortex contributes to planning, inhibition, attention and long-term goals. The orbitofrontal and ventromedial prefrontal regions help evaluate reward, risk and social value. The anterior cingulate cortex contributes to conflict monitoring and error detection. The amygdala is important for threat and emotional salience; the hippocampus supports memory and context; the insula helps represent internal bodily states, disgust and craving; and the hypothalamus helps regulate hunger, thirst, sexual drive, hormones and autonomic responses.

Habit and reward learning involve the basal ganglia and striatum. The ventral striatum, including the nucleus accumbens, participates in motivation and reward anticipation. Dopamine is important for learning, motivation and reward prediction; it is not simply a 'pleasure chemical.' The thalamus contributes to sensory relay and awareness, while brainstem systems are essential for arousal, breathing and wakefulness. The default mode network contributes to self-referential and autobiographical thought. These systems can influence pride, fear, lust, anger, greed, gluttony, envy or avoidance only indirectly through broader patterns of attention, motivation, memory, interpretation and choice; neuroscience cannot identify a 'sin centre' or measure moral guilt from a scan.

Neuroplasticity refers to changes in neural functioning or structure with experience, development or injury. Repeated practice can strengthen some patterns and make behaviours easier to initiate, but plasticity does not mean every difficulty can be changed by willpower alone. A sound account keeps biological, psychological, social and moral levels distinct while recognising that they interact.
units.assignment: Create a table with six brain systems (for example: prefrontal cortex, amygdala, hippocampus, striatum, hypothalamus and insula). For each, state one supported function and one claim you should avoid. Include why no region should be labelled 'the pride centre,' 'the lust centre' or 'the sin centre.'

quiz.question: Complex behaviour is best understood through what?
options: A brain scan that directly shows someone’s character.
Interacting neural, bodily and environmental processes.
One brain area for every moral quality.
quiz.explanation: Complex functions depend on networks and context.

quiz.question: What does neuroplasticity imply?
options: Experience can change aspects of the nervous system.
Every condition can be cured through willpower.
All change follows a fixed 21-day schedule.
quiz.explanation: Plasticity is real but does not justify universal timelines or cures.

units.title: Attention, consciousness and sleep
units.label: Educational study
objectives: Differentiate conscious awareness, easily retrievable preconscious information, automatic processing and theoretical uses of the term unconscious.
Explain why conscious, preconscious and unconscious are not three anatomical brain compartments.
Apply the lesson to the case study and explain the limits of your conclusion.
paragraphs: Conscious processing refers to what is presently available to awareness: current perceptions, thoughts, choices and deliberate attention. Conscious experience depends on distributed brain systems rather than one small location. Frontal and parietal association networks, thalamic interactions and brainstem arousal systems all contribute to the conditions under which experience can become conscious.

Preconscious is a historical psychological term for information that is not currently in awareness but can become available readily, such as a familiar phone number or a remembered appointment. Unconscious processing is broader and includes activity that influences behaviour without deliberate awareness, such as some learned associations, priming, emotional appraisals, procedural routines and automatic habits. 'Subconscious' is common in everyday speech but is not a single, precisely defined neuroscientific system.

A useful distinction is between automaticity and helplessness. A person may reach for a phone before fully noticing the urge, or feel fear before consciously identifying the trigger. That does not mean every later action is uncontrollable. Awareness can create an opportunity for reflection, inhibition and a different response. Sleep, fatigue, stress and divided attention can reduce this capacity, which is one reason behaviour should be understood in context rather than moralised immediately.
units.assignment: Draw a four-level diagram labelled conscious awareness, readily retrievable information, automatic processing, and theoretical unconscious processes. Explain why this is a functional model rather than a map of four separate brain locations.

quiz.question: How should the word subconscious be used in study?
options: Define the intended meaning and theoretical context.
Assume it names one anatomical chamber.
Use it as proof that all behaviour is uncontrollable.
quiz.explanation: Terms differ across theories and everyday speech.

quiz.question: Why might distraction reduce later recall?
options: Memory stores every event perfectly anyway.
Distraction proves a permanent disorder.
Information may receive less attention during encoding.
quiz.explanation: Attention affects what is encoded; a single lapse is not a diagnosis.

units.title: Learning and habits
units.label: Educational study
objectives: Explain cue, behaviour and consequence loops in habit formation.
Describe the roles of repetition, context, reward learning and automaticity without promising a fixed habit timeline.
Design low-risk habits for prayer, study/work and physical health.
paragraphs: Habits are learned patterns that become easier to trigger in familiar contexts. A practical model is cue → behaviour → consequence. The cue may be a time, place, emotion, preceding action or social context. The behaviour is the routine itself. The consequence may be pleasure, relief, completion, social approval or another outcome that affects future repetition. Basal-ganglia and striatal systems are strongly involved in habit learning, while prefrontal systems remain important for planning, monitoring and changing behaviour.

Reward learning is not the same as chasing pleasure. Dopamine helps encode prediction, salience and learning from outcomes. Some habits are reinforced because they produce pleasure; others because they remove discomfort. This is why stress can trigger scrolling, avoidance or compulsive behaviour even when the person no longer finds the behaviour deeply satisfying. Repeated pairings can make a cue evoke craving or action before conscious reflection is fully engaged.

For behaviour change, make the desired action small, attach it to a stable cue and reduce friction. A three-domain exercise can use: after morning washing → five minutes of prayer; after breakfast → ten minutes of focused study or work; after the main work block → five to ten minutes of movement. Record completion without self-punishment. On difficult days, preserve the minimum version. Missing once is information about context, not proof of a defective character or a failed brain.
units.assignment: Design a 30-day three-domain habit plan for spiritual life, study/work and physical health. For each, state the cue, minimum action, likely reward or relief, one friction-reduction step, and what you will do after a missed day.

quiz.question: What is an example of a clear habit cue?
options: Be a perfect learner from now on.
Punish yourself whenever you feel distracted.
After opening the textbook, answer one recall question.
quiz.explanation: A specific cue and manageable action make a plan observable.

quiz.question: What does a missed day establish?
options: The brain is permanently damaged.
The plan may need adjustment; it does not define the person.
The person can never change.
quiz.explanation: Review context and barriers before drawing broad conclusions.

units.title: Memory and effective study
units.label: Educational study
objectives: Distinguish encoding, storage and retrieval.
Apply the lesson to the case study and explain the limits of your conclusion.
paragraphs: Remembering involves encoding information, retaining it over time and retrieving it when needed. These processes are related but not identical. Familiarity with a page can feel like mastery even when a learner cannot explain it without looking. Retrieval practice reveals what can actually be recalled.

Try reading a short section, closing it and writing a brief explanation in your own words. Check against the source, correct errors and revisit the material over several sessions. Varying examples can help distinguish understanding from memorising one phrase. Memory is reconstructive and can be affected by suggestion; confidence alone does not establish accuracy. In counselling or pastoral conversations, do not pressure someone to recover hidden memories or tell them what must have happened. For study purposes, compare your own recall with the text rather than judging other people’s reliability from confidence or emotion.
units.assignment: Design a short recall-and-review activity for a Mariology lesson. Explain why repeatedly rereading the same page is not enough to check understanding.

quiz.question: Which activity directly checks retrieval?
options: Count how familiar the page seems.
Explain a passage with the book closed, then verify it.
Look at a highlighted page without attempting recall.
quiz.explanation: Retrieval practice checks access to the material.

quiz.question: Does a confident memory guarantee accuracy?
options: No; confidence and accuracy can differ.
Yes, in every case.
Only when the speaker is emotional.
quiz.explanation: Memory is reconstructive, so confidence is not conclusive evidence.

units.title: Emotion, stress and regulation
units.label: Educational study
objectives: Distinguish emotion, bodily arousal, impulse, deliberate action and moral evaluation.
Explain fear and anger as normal affective responses that can be regulated without treating the emotion itself as guilt.
Use simple coping skills without suppressing or moralising feelings.
paragraphs: Emotions involve subjective experience, bodily changes, appraisal and tendencies to act. Fear often recruits threat-detection systems including the amygdala, while hypothalamic and autonomic systems prepare the body for action. Anger may arise when a person perceives threat, injustice, frustration or insult. None of these responses is identical to the action that follows. Feeling fear does not by itself prove cowardice, and feeling anger does not by itself equal violence or hatred.

The prefrontal cortex and anterior cingulate cortex contribute to monitoring conflict, reappraising situations and inhibiting actions. This means a useful practical sequence is: notice the trigger → notice bodily activation → name the emotion → pause → consider the situation → choose the next action. This sequence can fail under exhaustion, intoxication, severe stress or illness, so context matters. Regulation is not emotional suppression; it is increasing the range of possible responses.

When stress rises, a small pause can create room to choose the next step. You might notice the support of a chair, orient to the room, slow your breathing if comfortable, and name one manageable task. If grounding feels uncomfortable, stop and choose another form of support. Persistent distress is not a spiritual failure. Practical help with workload, safety, finances, sleep or relationships may be as important as an individual coping technique.

sources.title: WHO: Doing What Matters in Times of Stress

units.assignment: Use the sequence trigger → bodily response → emotion → conscious consideration → choice → action for one fictional fear or anger situation. Identify where regulation can enter without calling the emotion itself sinful.

quiz.question: Which statement distinguishes emotion from behaviour?
options: Anger can be felt without choosing violence.
Anger always makes violence inevitable.
Fear always proves moral failure.
quiz.explanation: An emotion and the action taken in response are different.

quiz.question: If grounding feels uncomfortable, what is reasonable?
options: Continue regardless of distress.
Assume you are doing faith incorrectly.
Stop and choose another support.
quiz.explanation: Coping practices should remain voluntary and adaptable.

units.title: Development across the lifespan
units.label: Educational study
objectives: Explain variation without using a stage model as a diagnosis.
Apply the lesson to the case study and explain the limits of your conclusion.
paragraphs: Development includes physical, cognitive and social changes across life. Researchers use different models to describe patterns, and each model has limits. A developmental milestone is a useful reference point; it is not a complete account of a person’s abilities or future.

Relationships, opportunity, culture, disability, health and economic conditions shape experience. Avoid judging an adult by one childhood event or treating older people as incapable of learning. When a child struggles, describe the observed difficulty instead of assigning a label after a brief encounter. A caregiver can seek advice from a qualified professional while also noticing the child’s strengths. In a learning journal, separate an observation (“needed the instruction repeated”) from an inference (“has no motivation”). That discipline matters at every age and protects against turning a general developmental theory into a stereotype.
units.assignment: Rewrite “This child is lazy” as a neutral observation and two possible questions for a caregiver or qualified professional.

quiz.question: What is a developmental model?
options: A diagnosis for every individual.
A guarantee of one life outcome.
A framework describing patterns with limits and variation.
quiz.explanation: Models support inquiry but do not replace individual assessment.

quiz.question: Which is an observation rather than a label?
options: The learner will never improve.
The learner asked for the instruction to be repeated.
The learner is lazy.
quiz.explanation: Observable descriptions avoid unsupported character judgments.

units.title: Personality, social influence and culture
units.label: Educational study
objectives: Notice situational explanations and avoid stereotyping.
Apply the lesson to the case study and explain the limits of your conclusion.
paragraphs: Personality describes relatively enduring patterns, while behaviour also changes with circumstances. A quiet person in one meeting may be talkative with trusted friends. Informal quizzes and personality labels should not become a diagnosis, a hiring rule or an explanation for every relationship problem.

Social psychology examines how other people and social settings affect thinking and action. People may underestimate situational pressures when explaining someone else’s behaviour. A missed appointment could involve transport, caregiving or confusion rather than indifference. Culture influences meanings and expectations, but membership of a group does not tell you an individual’s beliefs. Ask respectful questions and let the person describe their own experience. In a disagreement, distinguish the behaviour you observed, the interpretation you made and the additional information you would need before drawing a conclusion.
units.assignment: A volunteer misses two meetings. Write a curious, respectful conversation starter and identify an assumption you should avoid.

quiz.question: A missed appointment should first invite what?
options: A judgment about an entire cultural group.
A respectful inquiry into circumstances.
An immediate personality diagnosis.
quiz.explanation: Context may explain a behaviour better than a label.

quiz.question: How should a personality quiz be treated?
options: As limited information, not a clinical diagnosis.
As a complete prediction of all relationships.
As proof someone cannot change.
quiz.explanation: Informal categories do not establish clinical conclusions.

units.title: Mental health literacy and help-seeking
units.label: Educational study
objectives: Recognise when education should lead to qualified assessment.
Apply the lesson to the case study and explain the limits of your conclusion.
paragraphs: Mental health difficulties can affect feelings, thoughts, relationships and everyday functioning. Similar experiences can arise in different conditions or in response to stressful circumstances. Reading a symptom list is not enough to diagnose yourself or someone else. A qualified assessment considers duration, severity, context, physical health and other explanations.

Seeking help can begin with a primary-care professional or a qualified mental-health practitioner. Ask about credentials, experience, methods, fees, confidentiality and emergency arrangements. If someone is in immediate danger, needs urgent medical care or may act on thoughts of suicide, use emergency services rather than waiting for an online reply. In India, 112 is the emergency number; Tele-MANAS offers mental-health support at 14416. Outside India, use local services. Faith and community support can accompany treatment, but they do not replace needed clinical care.

sources.title: NIMH: Caring for Your Mental Health

units.assignment: Prepare three questions to ask a prospective therapist, and explain what you would do differently if there were an immediate safety emergency.

quiz.question: What can a symptom checklist establish on its own?
options: It can prompt further assessment, but cannot establish a diagnosis alone.
A definitive diagnosis for anyone.
The only appropriate treatment.
quiz.explanation: Diagnosis requires context and qualified assessment.

quiz.question: What takes priority in immediate danger?
options: Waiting for a course quiz result.
Continuing a long chatbot conversation.
Local emergency help and nearby human support.
quiz.explanation: An educational website cannot provide emergency response.

units.title: Integrating psychology, ethics and faith
units.label: Educational study
objectives: Keep scientific, psychological, moral and spiritual questions distinct and in dialogue.
Distinguish spontaneous emotion or temptation from deliberate consent and repeated chosen behaviour.
Explain how repeated actions can contribute to habits, virtues or vices without reducing moral responsibility to neuroscience.
paragraphs: Psychology can describe patterns of attention, learning, motivation, emotion, memory and automaticity. Moral theology asks about the human act, freedom, knowledge, consent and the good. Spiritual accompaniment concerns a person’s relationship with God. These questions can illuminate one another without being interchangeable. A symptom is not a reliable sign of sin, demonic influence or lack of faith, and a brain scan cannot determine guilt, virtue or sanctity.

A useful integrative sequence is: trigger or situation → automatic bodily or emotional response → thought, image or desire → conscious consideration → consent or refusal → action → repetition → habit. The early stages can arise without deliberate choice. This is important when considering fear, anger, sexual arousal, intrusive thoughts or cravings. From a Catholic moral perspective, temptation or spontaneous passion is not identical to deliberate consent. Moral responsibility concerns the human act as a whole and is affected by knowledge, freedom and circumstances.

Repeated chosen actions can form stable dispositions. Psychology describes learned automaticity and reinforcement; classical moral theology speaks of habits, virtues and vices. These are related but not identical vocabularies. Pride, greed, lust, envy, gluttony, anger and sloth should therefore be discussed as moral patterns involving the person, not as labels attached to a single brain structure. For example, reward systems may participate in craving, hypothalamic systems in appetite, and threat systems in anger or fear, but the moral evaluation of a human act cannot be read directly from those mechanisms.

Catholic teaching also distinguishes the passions from sin itself: emotions can incline action but are not morally good or evil in themselves apart from their relation to reason and will. A responsible formation approach therefore avoids shaming involuntary reactions, strengthens reflective freedom, encourages virtue through repeated good action, and recognises when psychological or medical help is needed.

sources.title: Catechism of the Catholic Church §§1730–1742: Human freedom
Catechism of the Catholic Church §§1762–1775: The passions
Catechism of the Catholic Church §§1803–1845: Virtues
Catechism of the Catholic Church §§1846–1876: Sin

units.assignment: Case: a person feels a sudden surge of anger and has an insulting thought, but pauses before acting. Analyse the case under five headings: automatic response, conscious awareness, possible consent, chosen action, and habit formation. Then explain why neither the emotion nor one brain region determines moral guilt.

quiz.question: What does a mental-health symptom prove about someone’s faith?
options: It proves possession.
It proves prayer has failed.
It does not establish spiritual failure or moral guilt.
quiz.explanation: Clinical experiences should not be treated as evidence of spiritual guilt.

quiz.question: What is a responsible outcome of this introductory course?
options: Authority to stop someone’s medication.
Better understanding and appropriate help-seeking.
Permission to diagnose or practise psychotherapy.
quiz.explanation: Education does not confer clinical competence or registration.

units.title: Sensation and perception
units.label: Professional-style psychology formation
objectives: Distinguish sensation from perception.
Explain thresholds, adaptation and top-down processing.
Describe perceptual errors without treating them as character defects.
paragraphs: Sensation concerns detection of physical energy by sensory systems; perception concerns the brain's organization and interpretation of sensory input. The two processes are deeply integrated rather than sequential boxes.

Perception is constructive. Expectations, attention, context and prior learning influence what is noticed and how ambiguous information is interpreted. This does not mean reality is arbitrary; perceptual systems make constrained inferences from incomplete information.

Visual, auditory, somatosensory, olfactory and gustatory systems use different receptors and neural pathways. Professional study connects receptor physiology, neural coding and psychological experience.

lectureSections.title: Perceptual organization
paragraphs: Study figure-ground organization, depth cues, constancies, Gestalt grouping, signal detection and multisensory integration. Distinguish ordinary illusions from hallucinations or clinical symptoms, which require context and assessment.

units.assignment: Analyze one visual or auditory illusion, explaining the perceptual mechanism and why an illusion is not evidence of mental disorder.

quiz.question: Perception is best described as what?
options: Organization and interpretation of sensory input
Perfect recording of reality
A moral judgment
quiz.explanation: Perception constructs meaningful experience from sensory information.

quiz.question: Top-down processing can be influenced by expectations.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Prior knowledge and expectation can shape perception.

units.title: Motivation, reward and self-regulation
units.label: Professional-style psychology formation
objectives: Compare drive, incentive, expectancy and self-determination accounts.
Explain reward prediction without reducing motivation to dopamine.
Design motivation strategies that preserve autonomy.
paragraphs: Motivation includes processes that energize, direct and sustain behavior. Biological needs, learned incentives, goals, social context, identity and expectations can all contribute.

Dopamine participates in reward prediction, salience and learning. It does not map neatly onto pleasure, happiness or moral goodness. A person may strongly 'want' an outcome without strongly 'liking' it.

Self-regulation includes goal representation, monitoring, inhibition, environmental design and recovery after setbacks. Sustainable change often depends more on structure and repetition than on fluctuating motivation.

lectureSections.title: Intrinsic and extrinsic motivation
paragraphs: External rewards can be useful, but autonomy, competence and relatedness also matter. In education or ministry, avoid manipulation and excessive reward structures that undermine ownership of the task.

units.assignment: Design a motivation plan for a month-long study goal using environmental cues, intrinsic reasons, feedback and a recovery plan.

quiz.question: Dopamine is simply the brain's pleasure chemical.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Dopamine has broader roles in learning, salience and motivation.

quiz.question: Self-regulation includes environmental design.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Changing cues and friction can support behavior.

units.title: Thinking, language and decision-making
units.label: Professional-style psychology formation
objectives: Explain concepts, schemas, heuristics and problem solving.
Describe common cognitive biases without using them as insults.
Analyze language as a cognitive and social system.
paragraphs: Cognition includes categorization, reasoning, problem solving, judgment, imagination and language. Human thinking is efficient partly because it uses heuristics—shortcuts that often work but can also produce systematic errors.

Biases such as availability, anchoring and confirmation bias are tendencies, not diagnoses. Naming a bias does not by itself prove that another person's conclusion is false; the actual evidence and argument still matter.

Language enables symbolic thought and social coordination. Research examines phonology, syntax, semantics, pragmatics and language development, while debates continue about how language and thought influence one another.

lectureSections.title: Decision architecture
paragraphs: Professional analysis distinguishes the quality of the decision process from the eventual outcome. A good decision can have a bad outcome under uncertainty, and a poor decision can occasionally succeed by chance.

units.assignment: Analyze a fictional decision using at least three possible biases, then state what evidence would be needed before concluding that any bias actually occurred.

quiz.question: A heuristic is always irrational.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Heuristics can be efficient but sometimes biased.

quiz.question: Naming a cognitive bias automatically disproves a person's conclusion.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: The evidence and argument still need evaluation.

units.title: Attachment, relationships and interpersonal development
units.label: Professional-style psychology formation
objectives: Explain attachment as a developmental framework rather than a fixed identity label.
Describe relational regulation and interpersonal expectations.
Avoid overinterpreting popular attachment quizzes.
paragraphs: Attachment research examines how children use caregivers as sources of safety and how patterns of responsiveness relate to exploration and distress regulation. Adult attachment research extends some concepts to close relationships but uses different methods and constructs.
Attachment categories are probabilistic descriptions, not permanent destinies. Relationships, therapy, development and life circumstances can change interpersonal expectations and behavior.
Professional use requires attention to culture, family structure, developmental stage and measurement method. Casual labels such as 'avoidant person' can obscure context and reinforce stereotypes.

lectureSections.title: Relational skills
paragraphs: Listening, repair after conflict, boundary setting, emotional communication and mutual responsiveness can be studied behaviorally without pretending to infer another person's entire inner attachment history.

units.assignment: Write a case formulation that uses attachment concepts cautiously while listing at least three alternative explanations for the person's behavior.

quiz.question: Attachment style is an unchangeable personality destiny.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Attachment patterns are not immutable labels.

quiz.question: Cultural and family context matter in attachment interpretation.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Attachment measures and behavior must be interpreted in context.

units.title: Trauma, adversity and resilience
units.label: Professional-style psychology formation
objectives: Define traumatic exposure and trauma-related responses carefully.
Explain resilience without romanticizing suffering.
Distinguish supportive care from trauma treatment.
paragraphs: Trauma-related responses can involve intrusive memories, avoidance, hyperarousal, negative mood, dissociation or bodily distress, but exposure and response vary widely. Not everyone who experiences adversity develops a disorder.

Resilience is not invulnerability. It can involve relationships, meaning, material stability, coping skills, community, treatment and time. Calling someone 'resilient' should never excuse unsafe conditions or deny support.

Supportive listeners should avoid pressuring a person to recount traumatic details, claiming recovered memories, or interpreting distress as spiritual failure. Trauma-focused treatment requires appropriately trained clinicians.
units.assignment: Create a trauma-informed support plan for a fictional community member, including what a volunteer should not do and when referral is appropriate.

quiz.question: Everyone exposed to adversity develops PTSD.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Responses vary and diagnosis requires assessment.

quiz.question: Trauma-informed support includes choice and safety.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: These are core trauma-informed principles.

units.title: Psychopathology: classification, formulation and diagnostic limits
units.label: Professional-style psychology formation
objectives: Explain what diagnostic systems do and do not do.
Distinguish symptom, syndrome, diagnosis and formulation.
Avoid self-diagnosis from isolated checklists.
paragraphs: Psychopathology studies patterns of psychological distress and impairment. Diagnostic systems group symptoms using operational criteria to improve communication and research, but categories are not complete descriptions of persons.

A diagnosis considers duration, severity, impairment, exclusion of medical or substance causes, developmental context and differential possibilities. Similar symptoms can occur in multiple conditions.
Formulation asks how biological, psychological and social factors may interact in this person's difficulties. It complements rather than replaces diagnosis when used by qualified professionals.

lectureSections.title: Diagnostic humility
paragraphs: Students should learn categories for literacy, not to label friends, parishioners or themselves. A course cannot confer diagnostic authority.

units.assignment: Compare diagnosis and case formulation, then explain why a symptom list alone cannot establish either.

quiz.question: A symptom checklist can establish a complete diagnosis by itself.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Diagnosis requires broader assessment.

quiz.question: A diagnostic category is a complete description of a person.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Diagnosis is one clinical tool, not a total identity.

units.title: Psychological assessment and measurement
units.label: Professional-style psychology formation
objectives: Explain reliability, validity and standardization.
Distinguish screening from diagnosis.
Evaluate tests according to purpose and population.
paragraphs: Psychological measurement translates constructs such as depression, anxiety, memory or personality into observable scores. A test can be reliable without being valid for the intended interpretation.

Validity is not a single permanent property of a questionnaire; it concerns evidence supporting particular uses and interpretations. Cultural, linguistic and population differences affect measurement.
Screening identifies people who may need further assessment. It trades sensitivity and specificity and can produce false positives and false negatives. Screening should not be presented as diagnosis.
units.assignment: Evaluate a fictional screening tool by asking what construct it measures, for whom it was validated, and what decisions should or should not follow from a score.

quiz.question: A reliable test is automatically valid for every purpose.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Reliability is necessary for many uses but does not establish validity.

quiz.question: Screening and diagnosis are identical.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Screening indicates possible need for further assessment.

units.title: Psychotherapies and evidence-based care
units.label: Professional-style psychology formation
objectives: Compare major psychotherapy families.
Explain evidence-based practice as research, clinical expertise and patient characteristics/preferences.
Recognize treatment boundaries for non-clinicians.
paragraphs: Psychotherapies include cognitive-behavioral, psychodynamic, interpersonal, humanistic, systemic, trauma-focused and other approaches. Different problems have different evidence bases, and therapeutic relationship factors also matter.
Evidence-based practice is not 'use the most famous technique.' It integrates best available research with clinician expertise and the person's needs, values, culture and circumstances.
Pastoral care, friendship and peer support can complement treatment but should not imitate psychotherapy without training, consent, supervision and appropriate professional role.

lectureSections.title: Treatment literacy
paragraphs: When reading treatment claims, ask about study design, comparison condition, effect size, dropout, follow-up, population and possible harms. Avoid universal cure claims.

units.assignment: Compare two therapy approaches for one fictional problem, focusing on evidence, mechanism, boundaries and client preference.

quiz.question: Evidence-based practice includes client values and clinical expertise as well as research.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Evidence-based care integrates multiple sources of knowledge.

quiz.question: A pastoral volunteer should provide psychotherapy without training if intentions are good.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Role boundaries and competence matter.

units.title: Health psychology and behavior change
units.label: Professional-style psychology formation
objectives: Explain interactions among behavior, physiology and social context.
Use behavior-change models without blaming patients.
Analyze sleep, activity, adherence and stress as health-related behaviors.
paragraphs: Health psychology examines how behavior, cognition, stress, relationships and social conditions interact with physical health. It does not reduce illness to attitude or imply that positive thinking can prevent all disease.

Behavior change models consider readiness, self-efficacy, cues, reinforcement, environment and social support. Effective interventions often address barriers such as cost, access, fatigue, caregiving or unsafe conditions.

Medical adherence is a collaborative issue. People may have understandable concerns, side effects, logistical barriers or conflicting priorities. Psychological support should not override medical advice.

lectureSections.title: Biopsychosocial analysis
paragraphs: For a health behavior, identify biological constraints, psychological processes, family/social influences, environmental barriers and health-system factors before proposing individual motivation as the solution.

units.assignment: Create a biopsychosocial behavior-change plan for sleep or physical activity, explicitly avoiding medical claims or blame.

quiz.question: Health psychology teaches that illness is mainly caused by negative thinking.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Health is shaped by multiple biological and contextual factors.

quiz.question: Practical barriers can affect adherence.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Access, side effects and circumstances matter.

units.title: Professional ethics, culture and psychology-faith integration capstone
units.label: Professional-style psychology formation
objectives: Apply consent, privacy, competence and referral principles.
Practice cultural humility and avoid spiritualizing symptoms.
Integrate psychology and Catholic anthropology without confusing scientific and moral claims.
paragraphs: Psychological ethics centers respect for persons, competence, informed consent, confidentiality, avoidance of harm and responsible referral. Students of an introductory course should know these principles precisely because they are not licensed clinicians.

Cultural humility means asking rather than assuming, recognizing power differences and revising interpretations when new information appears. Religious belief can be a source of meaning and support, but clinicians and pastoral helpers should not impose faith interpretations on symptoms.

Catholic anthropology affirms dignity, freedom, embodiment, relationality and spiritual vocation. Psychology can describe mechanisms of emotion, habit and cognition; moral theology evaluates human acts; pastoral theology accompanies faith. Integration is strongest when disciplines remain distinct enough to correct one another.

lectureSections.title: Capstone method
points: Map biological, psychological, social and spiritual dimensions
Explain moral/spiritual issues without diagnosing guilt

units.assignment: Write a 2,500–3,500 word capstone case analysis integrating psychology, ethics, culture and optional Catholic pastoral reflection while maintaining clinical and moral boundaries.

quiz.question: Integration is strongest when psychology, moral theology and pastoral care are collapsed into one discipline.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: The disciplines should remain distinct while informing one another.

quiz.question: Cultural humility includes revising assumptions.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: It requires curiosity and correction rather than stereotyping.
